question: How do I trace a custom multi-turn agent in Python?

task_plan.description: Explain how to trace a custom multi-turn agent in Python, including how to capture multiple turns in a single trace or session.
task_plan.request_quote: How do I trace a custom multi-turn agent in Python?

outcome_assessments.answer_quote: wrap the whole session in `weave.start_conversation()`, and wrap each user–agent exchange in `weave.start_turn()`. Weave groups the turns into one conversation.
outcome_assessments.reason: It explains Python tracing of multi-turn agents and clarifies that turns are grouped by conversation, not one trace.

answer:
Use the Weave SDK's agent tracing helpers: wrap the whole session in `weave.start_conversation()`, and wrap each user–agent exchange in `weave.start_turn()`. Weave groups the turns into one conversation. Each turn is its own trace, not one big trace. [S1][S2]

**Steps**

1. Call `weave.init("TEAM/PROJECT")`. It authenticates with W&B and configures the OTel exporter that sends agent spans to the **Agents** view. [S3]
2. Open a conversation. `start_conversation()` stamps a `conversation_id` on every child span so turns are grouped in the Agents tab. If you pass your own `conversation_id`, keep it stable for the conversation's lifetime. Reusing the same ID adds new turns to an existing conversation. If you omit it, the SDK generates a UUID. [S5]
3. Open a turn per user message. `start_turn()` creates an `invoke_agent` span that becomes the root of a new OTel trace and represents one user–agent exchange. Called as a top-level function, it inherits the active conversation's ID. With no active conversation, the turn isn't grouped with other turns. [S7]
4. Inside each turn, wrap model calls with `weave.start_llm()` and tool executions with `weave.start_tool()`. [S4]

**Minimal example** (adapted from the quickstart; `call_model` and `run_tool` are placeholders for your own code)

```python
import weave
weave.init("TEAM/PROJECT")

def run_turn(history, user_message):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_message})
    with weave.start_turn(user_message=user_message, model="gpt-4o-mini"):
        with weave.start_llm(model="gpt-4o-mini", provider_name="openai") as llm:
            reply = call_model(history)      # placeholder: your LLM call
            llm.output(reply)
        # for a tool request:
        # with weave.start_tool(name="my_tool", arguments="{}") as tool:
        #     tool.result = run_tool(...)    # placeholder
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply

with weave.start_conversation(agent_name="my-agent"):
    history = []
    for q in ["First question", "Follow-up question"]:
        run_turn(history, q)
```

You still keep and resend your own `history` to the model, as the quickstart does. The conversation and turn spans only group what is recorded. [S4]

**Notes**

- The context-manager pattern closes and sends each span at the end of its block, even if an exception occurs. [S6]
- Weave keeps the active conversation, turn and LLM call in context. Helper functions in the same async context can call `start_llm()` or `start_tool()` without being passed a parent. [S6]
- The Python snippet above is illustrative and I did not run it. The full quickstart also shows recording token usage with `llm.record(...)`. [S4]
- If your agent uses a supported agent SDK, the docs point to autopatching integrations instead. [S1]

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

results.heading: Multi-turn conversations
results.snippet:
## Multi-turn conversations

Bedrock Agents preserve conversation state on the service side when you reuse a `sessionId`. To group multiple turns into a single trace in the Weights & Biases UI, wrap the turns in `weave.thread`:

```python lines theme={"system"}
with weave.thread("support-conversation") as t:
    for prompt in [
        "I can't log in to my account.",
        "I already tried resetting my password.",
    ]:
        ask_agent(prompt, session_id=t.thread_id)
```

Weave displays each turn in the UI as individual rows in the Threads view.

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

Use the Weave SDK's agent tracing helpers: wrap the whole session in `weave.start_conversation()`, and wrap each user–agent exchange in `weave.start_turn()`. Weave groups the turns into one conversation. Each turn is its own trace, not one big trace. [S1][S2]

**Steps**

1. Call `weave.init("TEAM/PROJECT")`. It authenticates with W&B and configures the OTel exporter that sends agent spans to the **Agents** view. [S3]
2. Open a conversation. `start_conversation()` stamps a `conversation_id` on every child span so turns are grouped in the Agents tab. If you pass your own `conversation_id`, keep it stable for the conversation's lifetime. Reusing the same ID adds new turns to an existing conversation. If you omit it, the SDK generates a UUID. [S5]
3. Open a turn per user message. `start_turn()` creates an `invoke_agent` span that becomes the root of a new OTel trace and represents one user–agent exchange. Called as a top-level function, it inherits the active conversation's ID. With no active conversation, the turn isn't grouped with other turns. [S7]
4. Inside each turn, wrap model calls with `weave.start_llm()` and tool executions with `weave.start_tool()`. [S4]

**Minimal example** (adapted from the quickstart; `call_model` and `run_tool` are placeholders for your own code)

```python
import weave
weave.init("TEAM/PROJECT")

def run_turn(history, user_message):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_message})
    with weave.start_turn(user_message=user_message, model="gpt-4o-mini"):
        with weave.start_llm(model="gpt-4o-mini", provider_name="openai") as llm:
            reply = call_model(history)      # placeholder: your LLM call
            llm.output(reply)
        # for a tool request:
        # with weave.start_tool(name="my_tool", arguments="{}") as tool:
        #     tool.result = run_tool(...)    # placeholder
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply

with weave.start_conversation(agent_name="my-agent"):
    history = []
    for q in ["First question", "Follow-up question"]:
        run_turn(history, q)
```

You still keep and resend your own `history` to the model, as the quickstart does. The conversation and turn spans only group what is recorded. [S4]

**Notes**

- The context-manager pattern closes and sends each span at the end of its block, even if an exception occurs. [S6]
- Weave keeps the active conversation, turn and LLM call in context. Helper functions in the same async context can call `start_llm()` or `start_tool()` without being passed a parent. [S6]
- The Python snippet above is illustrative and I did not run it. The full quickstart also shows recording token usage with `llm.record(...)`. [S4]
- If your agent uses a supported agent SDK, the docs point to autopatching integrations instead. [S1]
